title: Poor Proxies #3: The Feedback Gap
author: Jamie Clark
summary: Clark's third Poor Proxies piece targets the belief that students receiving attention, feedback and explanations are therefore learning. He defines the Feedback Gap as the distance between feedback given and feedback used, and leans on Dylan Wiliam's principle that feedback should be more work for the recipient than the donor. The argument is that detailed comments, praise without direction and next steps without lesson time produce workload without impact. He separates feedback as information from feedback as a recipe for action, citing Hattie and Timperley on its variable effects. The remedy is to build in time to respond, require thinking and revision, and judge feedback by the quality of the student response rather than the quality of the comment.
points: Giving feedback is not the same as learning from it, so the measure of feedback is student response, not the comment.
Wiliam's principle that feedback should be more work for the recipient reframes the question as whether feedback changed what students think and do.
Common failure modes include workload-style comments, praise without direction, next steps without time and re-teaching without checking.
Feedback functions formatively only when the learner uses it, so lesson time must be set aside to act on it.
Overwhelming or unusable feedback quietly damages confidence and leaves students feeling it happens to them.
quotes: The Feedback Gap is the distance between feedback given and feedback used. It's what happens when a teacher invests significant time and energy into writing comments, delivering explanations, and correcting misconceptions — only for that feedback to make no lasting difference to student learning.
Feedback is one of the most powerful tools in a teacher's repertoire. But it is also one of the most misunderstood.

This reframes everything. The question isn't "Did I give good feedback?" — it's "Did my feedback cause students to think and act differently?" If students read a comment, nod, and move on without changing anything — the feedback has not worked, regardless of how carefully it was crafted.

Wiliam distinguishes between feedback as information and feedback as a recipe for future action. Information tells a student how they did. A recipe tells them what to do next — and crucially, gives them the opportunity to do it.

This distinction exposes a common classroom pattern: teachers give feedback, students receive it passively, and the lesson moves on. Without a structured opportunity to respond, even the most insightful feedback evaporates.

The gap between giving and using is also where student confidence is quietly damaged. When students receive detailed feedback and don't know what to do with it — or feel overwhelmed by it — they disengage. Feedback becomes something that happens to them rather than something that helps them.

Closing the Feedback Gap isn't about giving more feedback — it's about designing feedback so that students are required to think, respond, and act on it. The goal is to make feedback the start of learning, not the end of marking.
